As of 230 AM EST Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry and unseasonably warm conditions continue 
today.

Surface analysis shows the area of high pressure that has been in 
control of our weather for the last several days now centered 
offshore. It will be pushed further offshore throughout the day 
today ahead of an approaching cold front, but the high will 
extend back west enough to give us another dry and unseasonably 
warm day today. Another round of patchy dense fog is occurring 
as of this writing, especially along the Eastern Shore and 
closer to the coast in SE VA/NE NC. Guidance tries to spread it 
westward over the next few hours, so it could be a foggy morning
commute. The fog will quickly dissipate after 8/9am and give 
way to a mostly sunny start to the day. With upper level ridging
overhead, temperatures will be able to warm a few more degrees 
than yesterday. Highs are forecast to reach the mid to upper 
70s, with the warmest spots being east of I-95. These 
temperatures are 10-12 degrees above normal for early November. 
Additionally, some light southerly breezes are likely this 
afternoon. Cloud cover will start to move in from the west this 
afternoon as the aforementioned cold front approaches the 
western edge of the state. These clouds will keep overnight lows
rather mild, only dipping to around 60 degrees for most 
everyone. Hi-res guidance is holding onto a low-end chance for a
few scattered showers for western locations overnight into 
Thursday morning. 

The first part of Thursday will be cloudy and mostly dry as we await 
the arrival of the slow-moving cold front. Again, there could be an 
isolated shower or two passing through during the day, but the 
majority of us will stay dry until late. Southerly winds will keep 
the warm temperatures around again, as highs top out in the mid to 
upper 70s. There could even be a few 80 degree readings in SE VA and 
NE NC. After a prolonged period of dry weather, dewpoints will rise 
into the mid to upper 60s throughout the day, so this increase in 
moisture will likely feel noticeable if you step outside. The dry 
pattern will come to a temporary end Thursday night.


KEY MESSAGE 2...Widespread moderate to locally heavy rainfall is 
expected Thursday night through Friday, with a few thunderstorms 
possible.

Confidence has increased as models have come into better agreement 
regarding a period of moderate to locally heavy rainfall Thursday 
night into Friday. The cold front will slowly move eastward as low 
pressure strengthens over the Great Lakes. This will result in rain 
developing across our western locations late Thursday 
night/early Friday morning, then expanding east by daybreak. 
Both the GFS and ECMWF depict a southwest to northeast axis of 
enhanced QPF extending from south-central VA up to the MD 
Eastern Shore. This locally heavy rain could be generally 
stationary over the same locations for most of the day, 
potentially dropping localized rainfall amounts of 2+". 
Confidence in exactly where those maximums will occur keeps 
shifting, but the possibility is definitely worth noting. 
However, the 00Z ECMWF is noticeably more east with the heavier 
rainfall than the GFS. 

Regardless, anomalously high moisture will accompany this 
system, with PWATs forecast to surge to 200%+ of normal for this 
time of year. There is also a slight chance of embedded 
thunderstorms on Friday, especially from mid/late morning through 
the early afternoon hours ahead of the cold front. Guidance is 
indicating 500-800 J/kg of MUCAPE alongside 40-50kt of shear during 
this timeframe, which could further enhance the areas of 
localized heavier rainfall due to the thunderstorms. The band of
rainfall will shift to coastal locations Friday evening before 
the front moves offshore in the early morning, bringing the 
rainfall to an end. Regarding high temperatures, the cloud cover
and persistent rain will keep most of the area from getting 
above 70; however, if the rain doesn't reach SE locations until 
the afternoon, then they may see another day in the upper 70s. 

A closed low pressure will drop into the northern Mid-
Atlantic/southern New England region on Saturday, reinforcing our 
northwesterly flow. This will allow drier and cooler air to fill 
into the area, dropping high temperatures back to more seasonable 
values. Highs this weekend will be in the mid to upper 60s on 
Saturday and low to mid 60s for Sunday. Overnight lows will drop 
into the mid to upper 30s (low 40s by the coast) each night. We look 
to remain seasonable and dry heading into the start of the new work 
week. Big model differences return late Tuesday.
